summary_grc: ὁ Θησεὺς μετὰ τοῦ δασμοῦ εἰς Κρήτην πλεῖ· ἡ Ἀριάδνη αὐτῷ λίνον δίδωσιν· ὁ δὲ Αἰγεὺς τὸ μέλαν ἱστίον ἰδὼν ἑαυτὸν ῥίπτει.
summary_en: The Epitome of Apollodorus 1.7–10, lightly adapted: Theseus sails with the tribute of young Athenians to Crete, Ariadne gives him a thread, he kills the Minotaur, loses Ariadne on Naxos, and forgets the white sail. Two sentences of ours set the scene.
caption_grc: τοῦτο ἐξάψας Θησεὺς τῆς θύρας ἐφελκόμενος εἰσῄει.

original.note: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7–10, lightly adapted: the first two sentences are ours; after them there is one story sentence for each sentence of the original, with Dionysus' children cut. The end of the Library survives only in a Byzantine summary (the 'Epitome'), so the sentences are even plainer than Apollodorus' own. In the Perseus text a few words run together; we restored the spaces.

sentences.text: Μίνως ὁ τῆς Κρήτης βασιλεὺς δασμὸν παρὰ τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἐλάμβανεν· ἑπτὰ γὰρ νεανίας καὶ ἑπτὰ παρθένους οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τῷ Μινωταύρῳ βορὰν ἔπεμπον.

maidens, unmarried girls (ἡ παρθένος)
as food (ἡ βορά)

tauros

sentences.text: καὶ εἰς τὸν τρίτον δασμὸν τῷ Μινωταύρῳ συγκαταλέγεται·

σύν + κατά + λέγω (count) | συγκαταλέγεται (he, Theseus, is counted in with them)

λευκός (white) | μέλας, μέλαινα, μέλαν (black)

to reveal (μηνύω)

εἶμι | εἰσῄει (imperfect: went in)

striking (παίω)

εἰσῄει | ἐξῄει (went out)

ἐράω + gen. | ἐρασθείς (having fallen in love with)
snatched (her) away, carried off (ἁρπάζω)

κατά + πλέω | καταπλέων (sailing home, putting into port)
ἐπιλανθάνομαι + inf. (forget to) | ἐπελάθετο (aorist)

grammar.md:
**Reading the Epitome.** The last part of the *Library* survives only as a Byzantine summary, so the sentences are short and bare: subject, participle, verb. What remains is exactly the grammar of the whole track.

**1. Genitive absolutes carry the plot forward.** Every step of the plan is an absolute: ἐχούσης δὲ τῆς νεὼς μέλαν ἱστίον (since the ship had a black sail), ὁμολογήσαντος δὲ … Θησέως (when Theseus agreed), ὑποθεμένου δὲ ἐκείνου (when he, Daedalus, had made a suggestion).

**2. Commands and conditions inside commands.** ἐνετείλατο, ἐὰν ὑποστρέφῃ ζῶν, λευκοῖς πετάσαι … ἱστίοις 'he told him, if he came back alive, to rig the ship with white sails'. The command is an infinitive (πετάσαι); the condition inside keeps ἐάν + subjunctive. Ariadne's offer works the same way: ἐπαγγέλλεται συμπράσσειν, ἐὰν ὁμολογήσῃ … ἕξειν.

**3. The historic present, again.** συγκαταλέγεται, ἐπαγγέλλεται, δεῖται, δίδωσι, ἀφικνεῖται: the story jumps into the present at each new step, and back to the aorist for the climaxes (ἀπέκτεινεν, ἥρπασε, ἐπελάθετο).

**4. Later Greek to recognise.** συμπράσσειν (Attic συμπράττειν); ἀπολλέναι for ἀπολωλέναι; μετήλλαξε 'he died', short for μετήλλαξε τὸν βίον.

| Greek | construction |
|---|---|
| ἐπελάθετο πετάσαι | ἐπιλανθάνομαι + infinitive: forget to do |
| τῆς θύρας ἐξάψας | ἅπτω + genitive: fasten to |
| λυπούμενος ἐπ' Ἀριάδνῃ | ἐπί + dative: grief at, over |
| Θησέα νομίσας ἀπολλέναι | νομίζω + accusative and infinitive |

culture.title: Theseus, Athens' hero, and the ship to Delos
culture.md:
In the 5th century Theseus became Athens' own Heracles. His deeds covered the metopes of the 'Hephaisteion' above the Agora and a whole generation of cups, which often run round the outside in a strip-cartoon: the bandits of the Isthmus, the Marathonian bull, and in the centre Theseus dragging the dead Minotaur out of the Labyrinth. In 476/5 the general Kimon brought back from Skyros bones said to be Theseus' and buried them in a shrine in the city, the Theseion (Plutarch, *Theseus* 36). Thucydides himself credits Theseus with uniting the villages of Attica into one city (2.15). In other versions Aegeus threw himself from a cliff into the sea, which was named after him: the Aegean.

The myth also lived in ritual. The Athenians said they had vowed to Apollo that, if the young people came back safe from Crete, they would send a sacred embassy to **Delos** every year, and they kept a ship they claimed was Theseus' own, replacing the rotten planks for centuries. While that ship was away the city executed no one: this is why **Socrates** waited a month in prison in 399, and why his friend Crito comes to him at dawn with news that the ship is about to arrive (Plato, *Phaedo* 58a–c; *Crito* 43c–d, the dialogue you began in Lesson 12.3).
